extracted.intended_audience: researchers, clinicians, students and practitioners who are reading and critically appraising health research (including drugs and alcohol research)
extracted.subtask_description: Using the CASP (Critical Appraisal Skills Programme) checklists to evaluate the trustworthiness, relevance and results of different types of health research (systematic reviews, RCTs, qualitative studies, cohort/case-control studies, diagnostic, prediction-rule and economic evaluations).

rubrics_metrics.name: CASP Systematic Review Checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: A critical appraisal tool designed to be used when reading systematic reviews. The page lists the CASP Systematic Review Checklist as one of eight tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What is a Systematic Review? Frequently there will have been more than one study addressing a particular health question. In such circumstances it is logical to collect all these studies together and base conclusions on the cumulated results. However the same scientific principles as would be expected in the original studies need to be applied to the identification, sorting and analysis of potentially relevant studies. The most obvious sign that a review is systematic will be the presence of a methods section. Meta-analysis is the statistical process of combining the results from several studies that is often part of a systematic review.

rubrics_metrics.name: CASP Qualitative Checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: A critical appraisal tool for assessing qualitative research. The page lists the CASP Qualitative Checklist among the tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What is a Qualitative study? A qualitative study examines the experiences and beliefs of people from their own perspective. It can take many forms including in-depth interviews and focus-groups with analysis attempting to identify underlying themes. Verbatim quotes of participants can be used to illustrate these themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: CASP Randomised Controlled Trial (RCT) Checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: A checklist for critically appraising randomised controlled trials; listed on the page as CASP Randomised Controlled Trial Checklist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What is a Randomised Controlled Trial (RCT)? An RCT is a type of interventional or experimental study design. Participants (individuals or groups) are randomly allocated to receive either the new intervention being tested or a control treatment (usually the standard treatment or a placebo). Each arm of the study is then followed up and the amount or severity of the disease measured in the intervention group and compared with the control group. RCTs are by definition prospective.

rubrics_metrics.name: CASP Case Control Checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: A checklist for appraising case–control studies; included in the list of CASP tools on the page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What is a Case-Control study? A case-control study belongs to the observational group of studies. It begins by choosing individuals who have a health outcome or disease whose cause you want to investigate. These are the cases. Controls without the health outcome are then chosen. You then determine the proportion of cases who were exposed to any risk factor of interest in the past, and compare this with the proportion exposed in the control group. The study is generally retrospective because it looks backwards in time to the earlier exposures of individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: CASP Cohort Study Checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: A checklist for critically appraising cohort (follow-up/longitudinal) studies; one of the CASP tools listed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What is a Cohort study? A cohort study, also known as a follow-up or longitudinal study, is another observational study design. In this study a population who do not have the health outcome or disease of interest are first divided into those who are exposed to a risk factor and those who are not. Alternatively exposed and unexposed populations may be chosen separately. Irrespective, both groups are then followed, often over long periods of time. At the end of the period of observation the incidence of disease or frequency of health outcome in the exposed group is compared to that in the unexposed group. The study is generally prospective as it looks forward from potential cause to consequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: CASP Clinical Prediction Rule Checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: A CASP tool intended for appraising studies of clinical prediction rules; listed among the set of eight critical appraisal tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page lists 'CASP Clinical Prediction Rule Checklist' as a tool designed to be used when reading research. No further details or examples are provided on this page.

rubrics_metrics.name: CASP Diagnostic Checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: A checklist for appraising diagnostic accuracy studies; included in the CASP tools list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The CASP Diagnostic Checklist is presented as one of the eight critical appraisal tools intended to be used when reading research. No additional explanatory text for diagnostic studies appears on this page.

rubrics_metrics.name: CASP Economic Evaluation Checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: A checklist for critically appraising economic evaluations (cost-effectiveness, cost-utility studies); listed among the CASP tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The CASP Economic Evaluation Checklist is included in the set of tools for reading research; the page does not provide further detail beyond listing the tool.

rubrics_metrics.name: General principle: apply primary-study scientific principles to reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic reviews should be held to the same scientific principles as the original studies they synthesize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When conducting or reading a systematic review you must apply the same principles of study design, identification, selection, and analysis that you would expect in primary studies; look for an explicit methods section as the clearest sign of a systematic review.
